transcript:
[00:00] Olivia Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — we wanted to run through a tight POC plan to pin down latency SLOs and how we'll measure them. Quick intros?
[00:10] Priya Kapoor: Priya, head of ML at Nimbus, we own model infra and evaluation.
[00:15] Dante Ruiz: Dante, platform — responsible for capacity planning and infra security.
[00:20] Marcus Diaz: Marcus, I'm Redwood SE, I'll lead the perf harness and benchmark design.
[00:26] Sophie Lang: Sophie, product, here to make sure the SLOs map to user-facing latency goals.
[00:31] Olivia Chen: Great. High level — we want to decide which latency metric matters for your product: TTFT (time-to-first-token) versus TPOT (time-per-output-token), or both. Also pick p95/p99 targets and acceptance rules for the POC.
[00:45] Priya Kapoor: For context, Nimbus runs a chat-style assistant embedded in our analytics UI. Most sessions have an average response length 80–160 tokens, ~70% single-turn, 30% multi-turn. Peak QPS today is around 60 across the cluster but could be 200 in peak sales demos. We care most about perceived latency for first token — users abandon if they wait >~600ms for the first reply.
[01:10] Sophie Lang: Right — product goal is first meaningful byte under 700ms for 95% of interactive queries. But we also get long-generation tasks (summaries) where overall throughput/cost matters.
[01:20] Dante Ruiz: Security note: any PII must not leave our VPC; if we do hosted, it needs private networking or dedicated. We also need KMS integration.
[01:30] Marcus Diaz: Noted. From a measurement perspective we usually capture both TTFT and token rate (TPOT) across a distribution of sequence lengths. For SLOs we recommend defining p95 for TTFT and p99 for TPOT for long-form workflows, but that's flexible.
[01:42] Priya Kapoor: Can you walk through the difference — I want to be sure we're not conflating them.
[01:46] Marcus Diaz: Sure. TTFT is the time between request ingress and the first model-generated token arriving. It captures initialization overhead, routing, model load, and any cold-start KV cache misses. TPOT is the per-token interval after the first token — so it captures autoregressive stepping throughput and influences total response time for long outputs. If you want snappy chat UX, TTFT is critical; for batch summaries or long transcripts TPOT and cumulative token cost is more relevant.
[02:20] Olivia Chen: I'll add a quick example: if TTFT p95 <= 600ms we hit the interactive bar; if TPOT p99 <= 120ms/token for 1–512 token sequences we can support long summaries without huge tail latency. Those numbers are just starting points.
[02:35] Dante Ruiz: How does batching affect TTFT? If you batch to save cost, won't TTFT jump?
[02:40] Marcus Diaz: Yes — batching trades off per-token cost versus TTFT. Continuous batching with latency windows can lower TPOT but may add a 30–200ms wait before first token depending on batch window. We'll model tradeoffs in the harness — Redwood Optimize provides guidance for batch window recommendations given your QPS and latency SLO.
[03:05] Sophie Lang: For acceptance criteria we prefer deterministic rules: e.g., during a 2-hour benchmark with production traffic replay, TTFT p95 <= 700ms AND TPOT p99 <= 150ms for sequences >256 tokens, with error rate <0.5%. Thoughts?
[03:22] Marcus Diaz: That's reasonable. I would caution that p99 for TPOT on >256 tokens could be noisy if we don't have enough samples. For p99 we need a decent tail sample — recommend either targeted long-run tests or synthetic amplification of long sequence traffic.
[03:38] Priya Kapoor: We can synthesize more long-form prompts; I'll ask the ML engineers to export a 48-hour window and mark the long sessions.
[03:46] Olivia Chen: On measuring: Redwood will run two bench modes in parallel — interactive (focus on TTFT under real-time QPS) and long-form (focus on TPOT under sustained throughput). We'll instrument both and provide raw latency histograms, KV cache hit ratios, token/sec metrics, and a per-request trace for a set of failed/tail requests.
[04:06] Dante Ruiz: For private deployment can you run the harness inside our VPC or do you need agents?
[04:10] Marcus Diaz: We can run the harness from your VPC if you host a small collector VM. Alternatively we can run in Redwood Dedicated with a network tunnel and we sign the connection. We'll detail both in the doc.
[04:24] Sophie Lang: Pricing/cost tradeoffs — if we accept slightly higher TTFT can we get 20–30% lower cost?
[04:30] Olivia Chen: Generally yes. Pushing higher batching or lower perf instance types reduces cost but raises TTFT. We'll provide a matrix: cost per 1k tokens vs expected TTFT/TPOT at representative loads.
[04:44] Marcus Diaz: Tooling: our harness will emit these metrics: request_id, timestamp_ingress, ttft_ms, tokens_emitted, per_token_ms (avg/median/p95/p99), kv_cache_hit (bool), model_variant. We'll also capture system metrics (GPU util, memory, context-switch counts) for root cause later.
[05:05] Priya Kapoor: On sample size — what's the minimal run length?
[05:09] Marcus Diaz: For TTFT p95 you can get stable estimates in an hour at your baseline QPS. For p99 you need longer or synthetic tail amplification — I'd plan for a 4–6 hour long-form run or a stair-step where we amplify long requests. For the POC acceptance, a two-phase approach works: 1 hour interactive baseline + 4 hour sustained long-form with synthetic tail generation.
[05:33] Olivia Chen: Timeline propose: Redwood sends harness and runner by 03-24; Nimbus provides logs by 03-22; we run benchmarks 03-25 to 03-27; results review and final acceptance 03-30.
[05:46] Dante Ruiz: From security side, we'll want to see an ingress-only setup — no outbound keys stored on the collector. Also need SOC2 evidence and a basic threat model.
[05:56] Olivia Chen: We'll attach SOC2 summary and a short KMS integration note with the harness.
[06:02] Sophie Lang: If we fail the SLOs, what are the usual remediation steps?
[06:06] Marcus Diaz: Typical steps: 1) check routing and collocated KV cache hit rates, 2) switch to a lower-latency model variant for interactive flows (we can route chat traffic to a smaller context model), 3) tweak batch window or enable prefix caching, 4) if necessary increase instance size. We'll include a remediation playbook.
[06:25] Priya Kapoor: OK — one last ask: can you capture percent time spent in model step vs scheduling vs network? We need a breakdown for cost allocation.
[06:33] Marcus Diaz: Yes — we'll add token-level breakdowns and a cost attribution sheet showing per-token GPU time vs infra overhead.
[06:40] Olivia Chen: Great. We'll follow up with the harness link and a sample runbook. Any other questions?
[06:47] Speaker 5: small side noise, sorry.
[06:50] Priya Kapoor: That's all, thanks.
[06:52] Olivia Chen: Thanks everyone — we'll email the artifacts and lock a follow-up.
[06:56] (meeting ends)
